title: Ishana Thakura, Servant of the Lord's Household
html:
A Servant in the Lord's House

In the house of Jagannatha Mishra in Navadvipa, where Sri Gaurasundara was born and grew up, there lived a servant named Ishana. He had served the Lord's father, carried little Nimai in his arms, served the Lord's mother, Shachi, all his life, and after Mahaprabhu's sannyasa he remained as the keeper of His house and the support of Shachi and Vishnupriya. He outlived almost all the Lord's companions in Navadvipa, and the next generation of acharyas — Srinivasa, Narottama, Ramachandra — found him a very old man in the same house where he had once dandled the little Gaura on his knees.

Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him simply Ishana; Vrindavana Dasa also calls him Ishana; Devakinandana in the “Vaishnava-vandana” calls him Ishana Dasa; Narahari Chakravarti in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” calls him Ishana, Ishana Thakura, “Sri Ishana Mahashaya,” “Ishana, dear to the Lord,” and “the Lord's Ishana.” The biographies call him Sri Ishana Thakura, Sri Ishana Prabhu, Ishana Dasa and “Mahaprabhu's family servant.”1

By position he was the household servant (griha-bhritya) of Sri Jagannatha Mishra; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” calls him “the servant in the Lord's house” (prabhura griha-bhritya); he is spoken of also as “the old servant of Sri Shachimata” and as one who served the Lord personally in His own home. But the word should not mislead us: this was no worldly post of a hired domestic. To serve the Lord in His house — to touch Him, feed Him and fulfil His wishes — is possible only for one whom the Lord Himself has chosen and who is dear to Him, for the Lord accepts service only from devotees dear to Him, and that service alone bespeaks Ishana's great fortune. He is a parshada, an eternal associate of the Lord who descended together with Him, and therefore he knew all truths (sarva-tattva-jnya), fully aware of the divine nature of the One he served; “his knowledge of all truths is known everywhere,” says the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.91). Ishana's service in the house of the Lord, of Shachi and of Vishnupriya is the eternal service of an associate in the Navadvipa-lila.

Of his origins the sources are silent. Neither Ishana's birthplace nor his parents, varna, or the year and day of his appearance are named anywhere; nor do the primary sources say who he was in Krishna's pastimes: he does not appear in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika.”2 Nor are the days of his appearance and departure in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

A Branch of the Chaitanya Tree

Krishnadasa Kaviraja, listing the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree, names him too:

“Srinatha Mishra, Shubhananda, Srirama, Ishana, Srinidhi, Sri Gopikanta, Bhagavan Mishra.” (CC, Adi 10.110)

In his “Anubhashya” to this verse (where Ishana is the fifty-seventh branch) Srila Bhaktisiddhanta cites three testimonies about him: the words of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” that Ishana served Ai, Shachi-devi, all his life and was the most fortunate in all fourteen worlds; the couplet of the “Vaishnava-vandana” on how Shachi Thakurani loved him; and the line of the “Bhakti-ratnakara”: “That Ishana is very dear to Nimai-chandra” (the twelfth wave, 12.95). These three voices — of Vrindavana Dasa, Devakinandana and Narahari Chakravarti — make up our story.

Nimai in Ishana's Arms

Ishana knew the Lord from His first days. When Mahaprabhu was born, Ishana would take Him on his lap and hold Him tenderly; later he carried the growing Nimai in his arms, bore with all His childish pranks and fulfilled all His whims. And Nimai grew so attached to him that He could not do without Ishana for a moment (eka-danda). An old brahmana of Navadvipa, whose meeting with Srinivasa we shall describe later, told him:

“How can I describe Ishana's doings? That Ishana is very dear to Nimai-chandra; Ishana's life is Shachinandana Nimai; without Ishana Nimai goes nowhere; in childhood Nimai was very restless — whatever whim He took up, Ishana would fulfil it.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 12.95–97)

These pranks and whims are no worldly mischief of a child but the sweet bala-lila, the Lord's childhood pastimes, and Ishana took part in them: the Lord Himself, the Master of all, allowed him to carry Him in his arms and to fulfil His wishes.3

Service to the Lord's Mother

Ishana is most renowned for his service to Shachi-devi. Vrindavana Dasa says of him:

“All his life Ishana served Ai; among the fourteen worlds he is supremely fortunate.” (CB, Madhya 8.74)

These words are cited both by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” and by Narahari Chakravarti in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.92).

Ishana knew that service to a devotee is higher than worship of the Lord Himself, and with great love he performed all the service in Shachi's house. And Shachi is no ordinary woman: she is non-different (abhinna-svarupa) from mother Yashoda, the Lord's eternal mother. This is no belittling of service to the Lord but the very heart of the Gaudiya Vaishnava path: service to His devotees pleases the Lord more than service to Himself. In serving Shachi, Ishana served the Lord as well, and the Lord was pleased with him; and the Lord's blessing follows the blessing of His devotee — the Lord's mercy comes by way of the Vaishnava's mercy.

And Shachi loved him dearly. Devakinandana Dasa sings in the “Vaishnava-vandana”:

“I shall praise Ishana Dasa with joined palms —
Shachi Thakurani loved him dearly.”
(“Vaishnava-vandana,” part 2, v. 37)

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” cites this couplet too (12.94); the biographies say that Ishana was blessed with Shachi-devi's love.4 Other “Vaishnava-vandanas” remember him as well: the Sanskrit one calls him “Ishana Dasa, the object of Shachi-devi's affection” (part 1, v. 50), the “Sri Vaishnavabhidhana” lists him among the Lord's associates (part 3, v. 16), and the tripadi of the “second” Vrindavana Dasa calls him “the vessel of Ai's mercy, Ishana, whom Ai brought up” (part 5, v. 37).

The old people of Navadvipa saw that love with their own eyes. That same old brahmana, meeting Srinivasa on the road, began his account thus: “I have just come from seeing Ishana. What can I say — who does not long for his virtues? His knowledge of all truths is known everywhere; he served Sri Shachi-devi as was fitting; and how Shachi-devi loved Ishana I cannot tell: I saw it with my own eyes” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 12.90–93).5

The Meal of Gaura and Nityananda

Ishana was blessed with service to Sri Nityananda as well, who is non-different from Baladeva — Sri Chaitanya's second self. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” tells how the Lord proposed to His mother that they invite Nityananda to a meal; Shachi rejoiced and began to cook, and the Lord Himself went to fetch Nityananda (Madhya 8.51–54).6 When the Brothers came and sat down side by side, Ishana came up to Them:

“Ishana gave water to wash Their feet; then Mahaprabhu and Nityananda sat down to eat.” (CB, Madhya 8.59)

Shachi was feeding Them when suddenly she saw both of Them as four-armed boys; she fell senseless, and the food was scattered about the room (CB, Madhya 8.62–72). It fell to Ishana to set the house in order:

“Ishana tidied the whole house, and all that was left of the meal was his. All his life Ishana served Ai; among the fourteen worlds he is supremely fortunate.” (CB, Madhya 8.73–74)

Thus all the remnants of the meal of Gaura and Nityananda — the greatest mercy — came to him; he honoured them with reverence.

On these verses Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Gaudiya-bhashya”: “Ishana, the servant in the Lord's house, gathered up the scattered food and tidied the house. There is no limit to Ishana's fortune: he spent his whole life in the service of the Lord's mother; and after Mahaprabhu's sannyasa the servant Ishana, obtaining the service of his Master's mother and wife, became the most blessed (dhanyatidhanya) among the blessed servants of the world.”7

Keeper of the House after the Lord's Sannyasa

When Mahaprabhu took sannyasa and left home to live in Puri, the care of His house, of His mother Shachi-devi and of His wife Vishnupriya-devi fell to Ishana. Together with him Vamshivadana Thakura was blessed with this service: both became the servants and protectors of Vishnupriya and Shachi.

Of the first morning without the Lord Vasu Ghosha sings. Shachi, waking, learns that her son has gone and lies as if dead: “striking her head with her hand, she gestures to Ishana: ‘Gora has gone, leaving Nadia’” (pada of Vasu Ghosha, “Pada-kalpataru” 2222). In her grief she cannot speak.

This is no worldly despair but vipralambha, the separation of the Lord's mother from her son — the feeling in which the eternal associates live when the Lord hides Himself from their eyes. And in that separation it is to Ishana that Shachi turns.

Yet even after sannyasa the Lord did not abandon His mother. He Himself told in Puri how on the day of Vijaya-dashami He came unseen to the house in Navadvipa and ate the food she had offered to Gopala. But Shachi saw that the pots were still full, and wondered:

“She called Ishana, had the place cleaned and plastered again, and once more offered food to Gopala.” (CC, Madhya 15.63)

Ishana remained in the house even after Shachi had departed from this world. After the disappearance of Mahaprabhu and the departure of Shachimata, Sri Vamshivadana Thakura served Vishnupriya-devi and Sri Ishana Thakura.

Srinivasa at Vishnupriya's

Soon after Mahaprabhu disappeared in Nilachala, the young Srinivasa came to Mayapur at the bidding of Gadadhara Pandita. At the Yogapitha, in the Lord's house, he saw Vishnupriya and beside her the old Vaishnava Sri Ishana Prabhu.8

The “Prema-vilasa” tells in detail of his care for the youth. Ishana, compassionate to living beings and ever filled with prema at the sight of a great bhagavata, noticed by a ghat on the Ganga an emaciated boy weeping and calling for Gadadhara Pandita. Ishana understood that Chaitanya's power was in him and told Ishvari — Vishnupriya — about him. With her permission he brought Srinivasa choice provisions; and when half a ser of rice cooked by the youth satisfied eleven Vaishnavas, Ishana told her of this too. At her bidding he brought Srinivasa into the inner apartments and presented him: “Here is Srinivasa; he bows down to you; he is your dear servant.” And afterwards he reported to her that the youth wept all night long, calling to Pandita Gosani, and never closed his eyes (“Prema-vilasa” 4.173–222).

Towards the end of one night Chaitanya and Nityananda appeared in a dream and commanded that Srinivasa be sent to Abhirama: “Send him to Abhirama, with Ishana as his companion.” The maids called Ishana, but he was fast asleep and did not hear; waking late, he thought himself most unfortunate, came with joined palms to Ishvari, at her word brought Srinivasa, and received the order to take him to Abhirama (4.236–244). This is the humility of a servant who reproaches himself for the slightest delay in service, not a worldly failing.

Their way lay through Khardaha. There Ishana announced a wondrous boy weeping at the gate and went out with Virachandra to fetch him; Jahnava, blessing Srinivasa, ordered a letter to be sent with Ishana to Abhirama. Ishana handed Abhirama the letter — “Ishvari's command: grant prema to the boy”; Abhirama seated him, sent him to fetch Srinivasa, and the next morning gave Ishana to Srinivasa as his companion on the way to Vrindavana (“Prema-vilasa” 5.11–64).

The Last of the Navadvipa Associates

Years passed, and one by one Ishana saw his contemporaries leave this world. When Narottama came to Navadvipa, Ishana, “dear to the Lord,” met him in the Lord's house: in great love he embraced the youth and said with tears: “It is good that you have come at such a time; from the Vaishnavas I have heard all about you” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.88–92). He touched Narottama's head and blessed him. Narottama also saw in Mayapur other aged associates of the Lord, grieving over His disappearance — Shuklambara Brahmachari, Murari, Damodara and Gadadhara Dasa. When leaving, Narottama asked Ishana's leave to go to Nilachala, and Ishana lovingly told him to go quickly to Sri Kshetra: “Day by day it grows darker everywhere. These days I have had all the news from there through people”; and how Gopinatha Acharya and the others now fare by the Lord's will “cannot be told.” And after that he advised him to go to Shrikhanda and Katwa (8.103–108).

When Jahnava came back to Navadvipa, Mahaprabhu's birthplace, Ishana was already a very old man; with others he consoled her, and they told her that Srinivasa would soon come (11.768). And earlier Srinivasa had told her: “In Navadvipa almost all have disappeared — only the Lord's Ishana remains,” and added: “Ishana told me to come” (11.721–723).

In the house of Jagannatha Mishra in Mayapur Ramachandra Kaviraja too, returning from Vraja to Gauda, found the very aged Ishana Thakura: he introduced himself and bowed at his feet, and Ishana blessed him generously. According to one of the biographies, Shyamananda (Duhkhi Krishnadasa) as well found the very old Ishana Thakura in Sri Gauranga's house: he bowed to him, and Ishana asked who he was and, having heard, blessed him.9

Guide through Navadvipa

Ishana's last great service was to show Srinivasa Acharya, Narottama Thakura and Ramachandra Kaviraja the places of Mahaprabhu's pastimes — he led them round the nine islands of Navadvipa. One of the biographies calls him here “Sri Ishana Prabhu, the venerable devotee of Mahaprabhu's household.”10

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” tells of this in detail. On the road to Mayapur the three met that same old brahmana: he said that he had gone that day to see Ishana and that Ishana had told him beforehand of their coming — he was waiting for them in the house of Jagannatha Mishra (12.107–108). In the Lord's house they found him alone: he was radiant, tears ran down his face, and he was calling: “Vishvambhara!” (12.112–115). Ishana embraced all three (12.117–118) and said that he remembered the places of the Lord's pastimes — what he had seen himself and what he had heard from the old people — and that this was why he had called Srinivasa through Narottama (12.126–127). “I am old and have lost my strength,” he confessed, “but now my strength has suddenly returned” (12.131). The next morning he led them through Nadia (12.134–135) and all along the way told them about each place, and at times sang padas (12.625, 701, 752, 772, 809, 849, 2117, 4031).

His old age and frailty are also a pastime. The Lord kept His eternal associate in this world in order to hand over Navadvipa through him to the next acharyas, and the strength that returned to the old man at the sight of Srinivasa is His mercy, not a worldly recovery. Ishana's solitude in the house where Nimai's footsteps once sounded, and his cry of “Vishvambhara!”, are the separation of an eternal servant from his Master. One of the biographies adds that when Ishana showed them these places they had already fallen into utter ruin — and from this one may judge how long he lived.11

Farewell and Departure

Ishana remained long in the Lord's manifest pastimes: he disappeared only after Vishnupriya-devi and almost all of Mahaprabhu's devotees in Navadvipa.12 The three acharyas received his loving blessing and embrace and took leave of him. Embracing them, Ishana could not hold back his tears; he wished to say something — and could not, and only by a sign of his hand showed that this was their last meeting (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 13.8–11).

And so it was. The acharyas went to Shrikhanda to Raghunandana Thakura, and there Srinivasa told Raghunandana: “In the Lord's house only Ishana remained — what power have I to tell of his endless virtues! On the way I heard from people's lips: Ishana Thakura has disappeared” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 13.20–21).13 The eternal associate had departed from this world into the Lord's unseen pastimes.

When exactly this happened is unknown: according to the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” in Navadvipa, soon after he had led the three acharyas through the places of the pastimes, after the Lord's disappearance. The day of his departure, like that of his appearance, is not in the calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Significance

Ishana is one of the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree and an eternal associate of the Lord. In him is found what rarely meets in a single life: he held the infant Gaura in his arms, and he it was who blessed the acharyas who carried Gaura's teaching further.

His life teaches that only one dear to the Lord can serve Him personally — and such service is itself a sign of the greatest fortune. All his life he served the Lord's mother, seeing in Shachi mother Yashoda, and thereby pleased the Lord more than he would have by worshipping Him directly, for service to the devotee is higher. That is why Vrindavana Dasa called him the most fortunate in all fourteen worlds, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta the most blessed of the blessed servants of the world. And finally, he shows that the Lord's mercy comes through the mercy of His devotee: the Lord blesses those whom His Vaishnavas have blessed first.

He remained in the Lord's house when almost all had gone, and preserved for later generations the living memory of Navadvipa.

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Ishana, the servant of Sanatana Gosvami (CC, Madhya 20.23–36); Ishana Nagara, the disciple of Advaita Acharya and author of the “Advaita-prakasha”; the Vrindavana Vaishnava Ishana, who was with Rupa Gosvami at Gopala's (CC, Madhya 18.52) and, according to the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” blessed Srinivasa, Narottama and Shyamananda on their way with the books; the kulina Ishana Bandya of the “Prema-vilasa,” and others.
  2. The “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (194–207) names a certain Ishana Acharya — in a list of associates, without saying who he is; by the order of the list the gopi Mauna-manjari corresponds to him (one of the biographies, following the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” — Yauna-manjari). No primary source identifies him with Ishana, the servant in the Lord's house.
  3. One of the biographies writes that Nimai lovingly called Ishana “father.” This is a misunderstanding: in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.95) the words “O son” (ohe bapu) are the old brahmana's address to Srinivasa, not Nimai's words.
  4. In the biographies this couplet is followed by “12.94” — the number of the verse of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” where it is cited; in Devakinandana's “Vaishnava-vandana” itself it is the 37th couplet.
  5. The edition used by one of the biographies reads “who does not understand” (bujhaye) instead of “who does not long for” (jhuraye). Some have taken the brahmana's words “I have come from seeing Ishana” as “here comes Ishana,” as if the brahmana were Ishana himself; but the account of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.88–109) makes clear that he is an old man met on the road, while Ishana was awaiting the guests in the house of Jagannatha Mishra.
  6. One of the biographies writes that the Lord long entreated His mother to let Him invite Nitai and that at last she agreed; according to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Madhya 8.51–52), Shachi rejoiced at once.
  7. One of the biographies speaks of “the rice scattered by Nityananda”; but according to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Madhya 8.67–68) the food was scattered when Shachi fell senseless (Nityananda scatters rice in another pastime — Madhya 11.15). Another biography cites verse 8.73 as evidence of Ishana's service after the Lord's sannyasa; in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” this is the episode of the meal, before the sannyasa, and only the “Gaudiya-bhashya” speaks of the service after it.
  8. One of the biographies refers here to the fourth wave of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” and to the “Prema-vilasa”; in the fourth wave of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” Ishana is not named — it is the “Prema-vilasa” that tells of him.
  9. The biography does not name the primary source of this account; it could not be found in the “Bhakti-ratnakara.”
  10. The biographies differ on the order of events: according to one, the three came to Navadvipa from Yajigrama after the festival of the Deities and Shyamananda's departure; according to another, they first went round Navadvipa and then went by way of Mayapur to Yajigrama, Shrikhanda, Budhari and Kheturi.
  11. This is the biography's own conclusion; the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.88–135, 12.4031–4037) does not say so directly, though Srinivasa does marvel there that the Lord's house is made of grass (12.4034).
  12. The biographies write that he outlived “all” Mahaprabhu's devotees in Navadvipa; but the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says “almost all have disappeared” (11.721), and of those who remained, “almost silent” (13.19); in Narottama's time Shuklambara, Damodara Pandita, Shripati and Shrinidhi were still living in Navadvipa (the eighth wave).
  13. According to the biographies, the news reached them when they came to Shrikhanda, or “soon after this”; according to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (13.21), Srinivasa heard it on the way.
